```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  eval = requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
)
```

Two long-standing requests on the 'sf' issue tracker ask for overlays that
pairwise clipping handles awkwardly:

* [r-spatial/sf#1959](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/1959) asks for
  an equivalent of the Esri *Identity* overlay: split the polygons of one
  layer by the boundaries of another and keep the attributes of both.
* [r-spatial/sf#2242](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/2242) asks for
  a faster and more robust n-ary intersection of a single layer: every piece
  of the plane with the number of polygons covering it, and which ones.

polymer answers both with the same two steps. `polymer()` puts every edge of
every input into one triangulation and records which features cover each
triangle, and `fuse()` dissolves the triangles into one piece per distinct
set of covering features. The rest is bookkeeping on the `origins` of each
piece.

This vignette also sets out where 'sf' and where 'wk' belong in such a
workflow. In short: prepare the inputs with 'sf', hand the 'sf' objects to
`polymer()` as they are, do the bookkeeping on polymer's own tables, and
convert back to 'sf' once, at the end.

```{r packages}
library(polymer)
```

## Where conversion to wk belongs

polymer reads anything the 'wk' package can handle, 'sf' data frames
included, and converts the geometry to well-known binary itself. Converting
an 'sf' layer with `wk::as_wkb()` before calling `polymer()` gains nothing:
the conversion takes a fraction of a millisecond for the example layers
here, and passing the 'sf' data frame lets polymer keep its attribute
columns and check that all layers share a coordinate reference system.

What matters is what has to happen *before* the geometry leaves 'sf', because
'wk' cannot do it:

1. **Project to a planar CRS.** polymer works in the plane. Edges are
   straight lines in the input coordinates and crossings are computed in
   those coordinates. With longitude and latitude the result is a valid
   planar overlay in degrees, but 'sf' measures the same polygons with
   geodesic edges (via 's2', or 'lwgeom' when 's2' is off), so areas and
   comparisons no longer line up. Use `sf::st_transform()` first.
2. **Repair and select.** Use `sf::st_make_valid()` if the input needs it,
   and drop attribute columns you do not want carried through.

After `polymer()`, everything needed for the overlay is already in plain R
structures: the layer attributes in `pool$layers`, the covering features of
each piece in `pieces$origins`, and the triangles in `pool$mesh`. There is no
reason to go back to 'sf' in the middle, for example to drop geometry with
`sf::st_drop_geometry()` or to measure areas. Pieces stay as `wk::wkb()`
until the end, where one call to `sf::st_as_sf()` gives an 'sf' data frame
for plotting, writing or comparison.

The example layers `soil` and `field` are in longitude and latitude, so they
are projected first, here to the European equal-area projection.

```{r project}
soil_p <- sf::st_transform(soil, 3035)
field_p <- sf::st_transform(field, 3035)
```

## Identity (sf#1959)

Identity keeps every part of the input layer `x`, split along the boundaries
of the identity layer `y`, with the attributes of both. Parts of `x` outside
`y` get missing values for `y`'s attributes, and parts of `y` outside `x` are
dropped.

With polymer that is a filter on the origins of each piece: keep the pieces
with a layer-1 origin, and look up the attributes of the layer-1 and layer-2
features listed there in `pool$layers`.

```{r identity-fun}
identity_pieces <- function(pool, pieces) {
  map <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pieces)), function(i) {
    o <- pieces$origins[[i]]
    fx <- o$feature[o$layer == 1L]
    fy <- o$feature[o$layer == 2L]
    if (!length(fx)) return(NULL)        # only in y: dropped
    if (!length(fy)) fy <- NA_integer_   # only in x: y attributes missing
    expand.grid(piece = i, x = fx, y = fy)
  }))
  out <- data.frame(pool$layers[[1L]][map$x, , drop = FALSE],
                    pool$layers[[2L]][map$y, , drop = FALSE])
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out$geometry <- pieces$geometry[map$piece]
  out
}
```

The function only touches polymer's tables, so it needs neither 'sf' nor
'wk' beyond indexing a `wk::wkb()` vector.

```{r identity}
pool <- polymer(soil_p, field_p)
pool
ident <- identity_pieces(pool, fuse(pool))
head(ident)
```

Now convert, once.

```{r identity-sf}
ident <- sf::st_as_sf(ident)
plot(ident["field"], main = "soil split by field")
```

### Checking against the pairwise workaround

The workaround in the issue intersects the layers, takes the difference of
`x` and the union of `y`, and binds the two. Written with base `rbind()`:

```{r pairwise}
pairwise_identity <- function(x, y) {
  x <- sf::st_set_agr(x, "constant")
  y <- sf::st_set_agr(y, "constant")
  inter <- sf::st_intersection(x, y)
  rest <- sf::st_difference(x, sf::st_union(y))
  rest[setdiff(names(y), attr(y, "sf_column"))] <- NA
  rest <- sf::st_set_geometry(rest, attr(inter, "sf_column"))
  rbind(inter, rest)
}
base <- pairwise_identity(soil_p, field_p)
c(polymer = nrow(ident), pairwise = nrow(base))
```

Both give the same pieces. Total area per combination of soil and field
values agrees to rounding:

```{r pairwise-check}
key <- function(d) paste(d$soil, d$field)
a_poly <- tapply(as.numeric(sf::st_area(ident)), key(ident), sum)
a_pair <- tapply(as.numeric(sf::st_area(base)), key(base), sum)
range(a_poly / a_pair[names(a_poly)] - 1)
```

### Checking with the mesh alone

The mesh can check itself, with no polygon geometry at all. Each triangle's
area comes from its three vertices, and `pool$index` says which features
cover it, so the area of every input feature is a sum over its triangles.

```{r tri-area}
tri_area <- function(pool) {
  v <- wkpool::pool_vertices(pool$mesh)
  t <- wkpool::pool_triangles(pool$mesh)
  i <- match(t$.vx0, v$.vx)
  j <- match(t$.vx1, v$.vx)
  k <- match(t$.vx2, v$.vx)
  ((v$x[j] - v$x[i]) * (v$y[k] - v$y[i]) -
     (v$x[k] - v$x[i]) * (v$y[j] - v$y[i])) / 2
}
ta <- tri_area(pool)
idx <- pool$index
by_feature <- tapply(ta[idx$triangle], list(idx$layer, idx$feature), sum)
range(by_feature[1L, ] / as.numeric(sf::st_area(soil_p)) - 1)
```

The triangles reproduce every soil polygon's area, so splitting by `field`
lost nothing.

### A point to settle

`expand.grid()` above gives one row for each pair of covering `x` and `y`
features. When features within a layer overlap each other, a piece is
covered by several features of one layer, and it is repeated once per pair.
The Esri documentation does not describe this case, and whether to repeat,
aggregate or reject such pieces is a choice for the caller. The soil and
field layers have no internal overlaps, so it does not arise here.

## One mesh, the whole overlay family

Identity is one of several two-layer overlays that GIS software offers
side by side: Intersect, Union, Identity, Erase and Symmetrical Difference.
Pairwise clipping computes each one separately, from the geometry. With
polymer they are all filters on the same pieces, decided only by whether a
piece has a layer-1 origin, a layer-2 origin, or both. The mesh is built
once.

```{r family}
pieces <- fuse(pool)
in_x <- vapply(pieces$origins, function(o) any(o$layer == 1L), logical(1))
in_y <- vapply(pieces$origins, function(o) any(o$layer == 2L), logical(1))
keep <- list(
  intersect = in_x & in_y,
  union = in_x | in_y,
  identity = in_x,
  erase = in_x & !in_y,
  symdiff = xor(in_x, in_y)
)
```

Pieces covered by a field polygon are filled purple, the rest grey.

```{r family-plot, fig.height = 3}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 5), mar = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", bty = "n")
for (nm in names(keep)) {
  wk::wk_plot(pieces$geometry, border = NA)
  title(nm)
  wk::wk_plot(pieces$geometry[keep[[nm]]], add = TRUE,
              col = c("grey80", "#5142A5")[in_y[keep[[nm]]] + 1L])
}
par(op)
```

Each filter's area agrees with the corresponding 'sf' operation on the
unioned layers:

```{r family-check}
area <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(sf::st_as_sfc(pieces$geometry)))
ux <- sf::st_union(soil_p)
uy <- sf::st_union(field_p)
sf_area <- function(g) sum(as.numeric(sf::st_area(g)))
cbind(polymer = vapply(keep, function(k) sum(area[k]), numeric(1)),
      sf = c(sf_area(sf::st_intersection(ux, uy)),
             sf_area(sf::st_union(ux, uy)),
             sf_area(ux),
             sf_area(sf::st_difference(ux, uy)),
             sf_area(sf::st_sym_difference(ux, uy))))
```

The filters work on any number of layers in the same way. A piece's
`origins` is the full record of what covers it, so any rule over layers
and features, such as "in layer 1 and layer 3 but not layer 2", is a
logical expression on that table rather than a sequence of clipping
operations.

## n-ary intersection of one layer (sf#2242)

For a single layer, `fuse(polymer(x))` is the n-ary intersection: one piece
per distinct set of covering features, with the count in `n` and the
features in `origins`. The example is overlapping discs, with one disc
duplicated, because the loop posted in the issue stops on duplicate
geometries.

```{r discs}
make_discs <- function(n, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  pts <- sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(x = runif(n, 0, 100), y = runif(n, 0, 100),
                                 id = seq_len(n)),
                      coords = c("x", "y"))
  sf::st_buffer(pts, dist = runif(n, 5, 15), nQuadSegs = 12)
}
discs <- make_discs(60)
discs <- rbind(discs, discs[1, ])

pool <- polymer(discs)
pool
pieces <- fuse(pool)
table(pieces$n)
```

The duplicate needs no special handling: discs 1 and 61 cover the same
triangles, so they appear together in the origins of every piece inside
disc 1.

```{r duplicate}
has_both <- vapply(pieces$origins,
                   function(o) all(c(1, 61) %in% o$feature), logical(1))
pieces$origins[[which(has_both)[1L]]]
```

The input `id` column is in `pool$layers`, so mapping origins to ids is again
plain indexing. Then convert once and plot the overlap count.

```{r nary-sf}
pieces$ids <- lapply(pieces$origins, function(o) pool$layers[[1L]]$id[o$feature])
nary <- sf::st_as_sf(pieces[c("n", "ids", "geometry")])
plot(nary["n"], main = "overlap count")
```

### Checking against st_intersection()

`sf::st_intersection()` on one layer computes the same partition. It returns
one row per piece, and can include points, lines and collections where
boundaries touch, while polymer returns one MULTIPOLYGON per covering set,
so rows do not compare directly. Area per overlap count does:

```{r nary-check}
sf_nary <- sf::st_intersection(discs)
types <- table(sf::st_geometry_type(sf_nary))
types[types > 0]

a_poly <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(nary))
rbind(polymer = tapply(a_poly, nary$n, sum),
      sf = tapply(as.numeric(sf::st_area(sf_nary)), sf_nary$n.overlaps, sum))
```

Because the pieces partition the covered area, two more identities hold:
area weighted by overlap count equals the summed area of the discs, and
plain area equals the area of their union.

```{r nary-identities}
c(sum(nary$n * a_poly) / sum(as.numeric(sf::st_area(discs))),
  sum(a_poly) / as.numeric(sf::st_area(sf::st_union(discs)))) - 1
```

### Timing

The reason for the issue is speed. The timings below were recorded once
(on a Linux cloud machine, GEOS 3.12.1) rather than run when the vignette is
built, because the 'sf' call becomes slow as the number of discs grows.

```{r timing, eval = FALSE}
for (k in c(50, 100, 200)) {
  p <- make_discs(k, seed = k)
  t_mesh <- system.time(pool <- polymer(p))[["elapsed"]]
  t_fuse <- system.time(fuse(pool))[["elapsed"]]
  t_sf <- system.time(r <- sf::st_intersection(p))[["elapsed"]]
  cat(k, t_mesh, t_mesh + t_fuse, t_sf, nrow(r), nrow(fuse(pool)), "\n")
}
```

| discs | `polymer()` (s) | `polymer()` + `fuse()` (s) | `st_intersection()` (s) | sf rows | polymer pieces |
|------:|----------------:|---------------------------:|------------------------:|--------:|---------------:|
|    50 |            0.04 |                       0.18 |                    0.07 |     222 |            201 |
|   100 |            0.06 |                       0.43 |                    1.38 |    1611 |           1059 |
|   200 |            0.24 |                       1.32 |                   71.99 |   19199 |           4467 |

For small inputs the two are comparable, and for the Identity example above
the pairwise 'sf' route is faster. As overlaps multiply, the cost of
pairwise clipping grows much faster than the cost of one triangulation.
Most of polymer's time is in `fuse()`, which rebuilds polygons from the
mesh; the mesh and its index alone, enough for counts and areas, are
cheaper still.

## Precision

Crossings are computed in double precision, and vertices are shared on exact
coordinate equality. The pieces form a partition by construction, so they
cannot overlap or leave gaps between each other, but the position of each
crossing carries ordinary floating-point rounding. polymer does not use
exact arithmetic.
